chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
title: Mercury foxtrot-tempo records like "Call of the Mambo King"
summary: Companies made them guinea pigs, simplifying with familiar melodies like "Donkey Serenade" over Cuban rhythm, and the records sold.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Macho, there was recordings from Mercury, some 78's like "Call of the Mambo King", which was very nice.
..... they were like in foxtrot tempos. Why did you record those, in those tempos, without any picante in it? Was there a reason for it?

Well, you know, companies they make like experiments. We was the guinea pig of practically every company that we have ever been and we was hungry to be recognized. Like a club fighter become popular and the manager want to make him an standard fighter ......
But weren't you playing this type of music at Concord and the people were loving it?
In other words, when you were at the Concord, you weren't playing your tipica music, you were playing a different book for the people at the Concord?
Did they like it softer, when you played it?

Oh, yes. It seems that when you play a melody on top, the people that doesn't know what the rhythm section is doing in order to -- You simplify the acceptance when you play a melody that they could recognize. "Donkey Serenade" was a standard number, so the people automatically they were dancing with the number "Donkey Serenade" because they know the melody. While we were doing all the complicated

rhythms that our rhythm section had, they never accept them because they had something to hold on. That's why all those American companies, because they are smart, they know marketing - this country is a mass-production country - and simplify the scene in order to make the people buy the, whatever they manufacture; so they suggest to us: "Machito, you want to record "Call of the Mambo King"? Sure. "You want to record "Affair to Remember"? Sure, why not?
"Sundown", all those kind of things. There was a ballad, we had Cuban rhythm and then with the American melody on top.
